extracted.intended_audience: photojournalists, journalism students, editors, photographers, and media professionals interested in ethics of image-making
extracted.subtask_description: Guidelines and evaluative criteria for ethical photojournalism and acceptable vs. unethical digital manipulation, including professional norms (AP code), core ethical pillars, case-study anti-patterns, AI implications, and relevant legal considerations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Truthfulness
rubrics_metrics.description: Truth is the cornerstone of photojournalism and ethical photography. The imagery must reflect what truly happened without alteration or misleading elements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensures the story behind the photo remains honest and uncorrupted by personal or corporate agendas. Photographs used in journalism should not be altered in ways that change the factual record.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accuracy
rubrics_metrics.description: Accuracy involves precise depiction of events without exaggerating or downplaying the visual facts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: It’s not just about what you show but also what you choose not to show; avoid selection or editing that could mislead the viewer about what occurred.

rubrics_metrics.name: Objectivity
rubrics_metrics.description: Capture and present images without personal bias, allowing the viewer to draw their own conclusions from unvarnished reality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Photographers should refrain from staging or directing events to fit a particular narrative; the camera should act as an impartial witness even though it’s operated by a human.

rubrics_metrics.name: Respect for Subjects
rubrics_metrics.description: Photojournalists must respect the dignity and privacy of the individuals they photograph.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be mindful of the potential impact of images on subjects; seek informed consent when appropriate, especially in sensitive or private situations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoiding Harm
rubrics_metrics.description: Consider the potential harm your work may cause to individuals or communities, both physical and emotional.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Take care to minimize negative impacts, particularly when photographing victims of trauma or violence; weigh public interest against potential harm to subjects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transparency
rubrics_metrics.description: Be transparent about methods and the context in which images were captured; disclose alterations when made.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Photojournalists should be accountable for accuracy and correct errors promptly. If an image is altered beyond accepted minor adjustments, that must be clearly disclosed.

rubrics_metrics.name: AP Code — No alteration except stated exceptions
rubrics_metrics.description: AP images must always be accurate. We do not alter or digitally manipulate the content of a photo or video except as stated below.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Minor adjustments acceptable: cropping without altering the context; dodging and burning; conversion into grayscale; elimination of dust on sensors and scratches on scanned negatives/prints; normal toning and color adjustments. These should be limited to those minimally necessary for clear and accurate reproduction and to restore authentic nature. Not acceptable: changes that substantially alter density, contrast, color and saturation; digitally blurring or eliminating backgrounds by burning down or aggressive toning; removal of 'red eye' is not permissible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Acceptable Minor Adjustments (author summary)
rubrics_metrics.description: Minor technical edits are acceptable when they preserve context and authenticity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Listed acceptable edits include: color adjustments, cropping without altering the context, level adjustments, sharpening, and noise reduction — all limited to what is minimally necessary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unethical manipulation — Adding or removing elements
rubrics_metrics.description: Adding or removing objects, people, or other elements to create a misleading context is unethical.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: photos altered to add or remove people (e.g., political images where subjects are removed/added), creating a false narrative. This changes the factual content of the image and is unacceptable in journalism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unethical manipulation — Cloning (copy/paste)
rubrics_metrics.description: Copying and pasting elements within an image to alter scene authenticity is unethical.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: duplicating soldiers or other elements to change perceived scale or composition of a scene (political ad example). Such cloning misrepresents reality and undermines trust.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unethical manipulation — Fabricating scenes (merging photos)
rubrics_metrics.description: Merging two or more photos to fabricate a scene or alter events is unethical.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: combining images to create a composite presented as a single real moment (Brian Walski LA Times case); photographers can be fired or disqualified for this practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unethical manipulation — Cropping to alter context
rubrics_metrics.description: Cropping that changes the context or meaning of a photograph is unethical.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: removing elements via cropping (and additional edits) to make a scene more dramatic; contest disqualifications have occurred when cropping altered story context (World Press Photo case).

rubrics_metrics.name: Unethical manipulation — Distorting proportions or repositioning elements
rubrics_metrics.description: Altering scale, proportion, or repositioning elements to fit layout or aesthetics at the expense of factual accuracy is unethical.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: moving the pyramids of Giza on a magazine cover to fit vertical layout — raises questions about altering images for aesthetic needs over factual representation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unethical manipulation — Changing facial expressions or body parts
rubrics_metrics.description: Editing facial expressions or body parts (e.g., via neural filters or AI) to modify emotional impact is unethical.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: AI and neural filters can change expressions (smiling, pouting, etc.); example of USA Today brightening a portion of a face altering appearance — such edits mislead viewers and are unacceptable for news images.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unethical manipulation — Exaggerating features to dramatize (smoke, fire, etc.)
rubrics_metrics.description: Adding or exaggerating elements like smoke or fire to dramatize events is unethical.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Adnan Hajj's Reuters images where smoke was amplified/duplicated. Such alterations exaggerate destruction and distort the factual record.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unethical manipulation — Manipulating colors to change mood
rubrics_metrics.description: Altering colors to materially change the mood or meaning of an image (e.g., adding blood color) is unethical.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: a tabloid altering a puddle to appear as blood — colorization used to deceive the audience is unacceptable in journalism.

rubrics_metrics.name: AI tools — positive uses
rubrics_metrics.description: AI can assist photojournalism by enhancing efficiency, accuracy, and storytelling capabilities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Uses include image analysis, tagging/sorting/organizing archives, detection/verification of authenticity, automated editing for technical corrections, and improved capture via AI-assisted cameras. These tools can augment a journalist's capabilities when used ethically.

rubrics_metrics.name: AI tools — risks and ethical challenges
rubrics_metrics.description: AI raises risks of manipulation (deepfakes) and bias, which can undermine journalistic integrity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Deepfake and face-swap technologies can fabricate visual narratives; reliance on AI for selection/editing may introduce bias. Vigilance, verification, and ethical guidelines are essential when using AI.

rubrics_metrics.name: Privacy laws (legal consideration)
rubrics_metrics.description: Photographers must be aware of privacy laws; photographing individuals in private spaces without consent can have legal consequences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Laws vary by jurisdiction; the use of intrusive surveillance equipment may be regulated. Always consider whether consent is required and know local rules.

rubrics_metrics.name: Defamation laws (legal consideration)
rubrics_metrics.description: Publishing false information that harms someone's reputation can lead to defamation claims.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Using a photograph in a way that misrepresents facts or links people to illicit activity can be legally actionable; ensure images are not used to convey false narratives about individuals or organizations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Intellectual property / Copyright (legal consideration)
rubrics_metrics.description: Photographers have rights to their work under intellectual property laws; others cannot use images without permission except where exceptions apply.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be aware of copyright, fair use exceptions (for reporting/commentary), and how rights differ by jurisdiction when reusing or licensing images.

rubrics_metrics.name: Trespassing laws (legal consideration)
rubrics_metrics.description: Accessing private property without permission may constitute trespassing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Respect property rights and obtain necessary permissions when applicable; illegal access can have legal consequences and ethical implications.

rubrics_metrics.name: Laws related to sensitive content
rubrics_metrics.description: Certain subjects (crime scenes, accidents, children) may be regulated by law regarding depiction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Know local restrictions on publishing images of sensitive situations and follow legal/regulatory requirements to protect subjects and comply with reporting laws.

rubrics_metrics.name: Press freedom laws (legal consideration)
rubrics_metrics.description: Some countries have laws protecting press freedom and ensuring journalists can work without undue interference.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Understand and advocate for press freedoms in your jurisdiction; legal protections (or lack thereof) affect how photojournalists can operate safely and ethically.

rubrics_metrics.name: Maintain public trust and preserve historical integrity (ethical goals)
rubrics_metrics.description: Photojournalism must uphold truth, maintain public trust in media, protect the reputation of outlets, and preserve the integrity of historical documentation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid manipulation that could manipulate public emotion or distort the historical record; ethical conduct supports institutional credibility and long-term trust.
